comment.value:
This paper introduces PARROT, a novel and comprehensive benchmark for Cross-System SQL Translation (SQL-to-SQL). The authors correctly identify that while Text-to-SQL has been extensively studied, the practical and frequent task of migrating SQL queries between different database systems (e.g., from MySQL to ClickHouse) remains under-explored. Existing benchmarks are ill-suited for this task as they typically focus on a single dialect (like SQLite) and fail to capture the rich, system-specific functions, data types, and syntax rules found in production environments.
The main contribution is the PARROT benchmark suite, which includes three variants of the datasets. The authors propose two execution-based metrics, AccEX (executability) and AccRES (result equivalence), to provide a robust evaluation framework. Their empirical analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) perform poorly on PARROT, with average accuracy below 38.53%, highlighting the benchmark's difficulty and the significant room for future research.

All reviewers recognizing the novelty and practical importance of the proposed benchmark. The reviewers praised the rigorous and well-designed data curation methodology, the paper's clarity, and its potential impact on the field.
There are several aspects where the paper can be further improved, including expansion of baselines and scope, deeper failure analysis, and the reviewers recognized the additional efforts made by the authors during rebuttal.

**Dear Chairs and Reviewers,**

We sincerely appreciate the time you have devoted to evaluating our work. Your thoughtful feedback and constructive suggestions have been valuable in strengthening our paper, and we are grateful for your recognition of our contributions.
- **Reviewer BoF9:**
> "the first large-scale benchmark dedicated to cross-system SQL translation ... construction process is rigorous and well-designed"
- **Reviewer hPXw:**
> "the paper is extremely strong and makes solid contributions to the field"
- **Reviewer tkLc:**
> "systematically studies cross-database SQL translation—an important yet underexplored task"
- **Reviewer Hp1m:**
> "addresses a practically important yet underexplored task"

We are pleased and grateful that our responses have addressed your concerns and strengthened the paper in the rebuttal phase.
Below, we summarize the key updates we will incorporate into the final version:

**1. Failure Analysis**

We have added a failure-mode taxonomy as well as a detailed analysis of different LLMs *(Reviewer hPXw-Q1, Reviewer tkLc-Q2, Reviewer Hp1m-Q1)*

**2. Baseline Scope**
- Added Gemini 2.5 pro results *(Reviewer hPXw-Q2)* and efficiency evaluations *(Reviewer hPXw-Q4)*
- Compared hybrid methods (rule-based+LLM) *(Reviewer BoF9-Q2, Reviewer tkLc-Q5)*
- Assessed different prompts and decoding strategies *(Reviewer Hp1m-Q2)*

**3. Equivalence Evaluation**

We have clarified evaluation details for handling limited coverage *(Reviewer tkLc-Q1)* and fully aligned schemas *(Reviewer Hp1m-Q3)*

**4. Benchmark Expansion**
- Clarified how open-source SQLs are transformed to mitigate LLM memorization concerns *(Reviewer hPXw-Q3)*
- Included safety and bias measurements *(Reviewer tkLc-Q3)* and extended support for complex scenarios *(Reviewer tkLc-Q6)*

Additionally, we sincerely appreciate Reviewer tkLc’s updated feedback to:
- Clarify $Acc_{RES}$ with per-dialect dataset descriptors
- Introduce per-capability leaderboards based on failure taxonomy
- Refine our repository with additional instructions including dataset splits, and complex scenario evaluations

We will also discuss recent NL2SQL methods in Section 6 *(Reviewer Hp1m)*.

Once again, we extend our deepest gratitude for your insightful feedback, which has been valuable in strengthening the paper's rigor, clarity, and overall impact. We sincerely appreciate the time and expertise you have contributed to this review process.

**Best regards,**

**The PARROT Authors.**

rebuttal.value:
**Dear Reviewer Hp1m,**

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback.
We sincerely appreciate your recognition of PARROT, and we take your concerns, such as failure analysis and schema handling, seriously.
We hope our responses help to address them and welcome any further questions or suggestions.

---

**▶ Q1. The case study is strong, but a taxonomy of common failure modes (e.g., date parsing, alias scope errors, aggregate translation) with frequencies could offer deeper insights.**

Thanks for the insightful suggestion.
To deepen our analysis, we have added a systematic taxonomy of failure modes based on real-world ByteHouse workload results, along with the error frequency distributions across different LLMs.
The identified failure cases fall into six main categories, which capture the types of errors raised in your question (e.g., "date parsing" refers to *Syntax Parsing*, and "alias scope errors" refers to *Identifier Resolution*).

- **(1) Syntax Parsing:** SQL statements that violate grammar rules, e.g., missing clauses or invalid keyword usage.

- **(2) Identifier Resolution:** References to undefined or ambiguous database objects, e.g., using a column name when multiple tables share the same field.

- **(3) Function Resolution:** Use of unknown or misclassified functions, e.g., calling a non-existent function or incorrectly treating a scalar function as an aggregate.

- **(4) Function Usage:** Valid functions called with incorrect argument types, counts, or values, e.g., passing a string where a number is expected.

- **(5) Type Compatibility:** Operations that combine incompatible data types or schemas, e.g., performing UNION ALL between two queries with different returned value types.

- **(6) Other Errors:** Miscellaneous issues outside the above categories, such as unsupported SQL features or incomplete syntax constructs.

Query migration is essential in numerous routine tasks, including:

- (1) Cross-database analytics tools that continuously translate SQL between heterogeneous systems to enable seamless, unified analysis;
- (2) Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) workflows, where SQL is used extensively to extract data from source systems, transform it through filtering, joining, or aggregation, and then load it into target databases with potentially different dialects.

For instance, at ByteDance, auto-generated queries from business intelligence tools require translation when migrating from Hive or Spark to ClickHouse database to ensure performance and compatibility.
This process sustains a production workload exceeding 1,000 queries per second (QPS) while adapting syntax, optimizations, and engine-specific functions.

**2. Reasons to focus on SQL‑to‑SQL rather than text‑to‑SQL.**

SQL-to-SQL is a more fundamental task that can serve as a foundation for a wide range of applications (e.g., data transformation pipelines, object-relational mapping tools, and cross-database interoperability), including text-to-SQL by translating their output (often tailored for SQLite) automatically into production‑ready dialects used across different enterprise systems.
In contrast, text-to-SQL is primarily designed for natural language interfaces and faces both technical challenges (e.g., semantic ambiguity, limited coverage of complex SQL constructs) and application constraints.

summary.value:
**Summary**
1. This paper introduces PARROT (Practical And Realistic Benchmark for Cross System SQL Translation), a new benchmark designed specifically for evaluating the ability of LLMs to perform cross-system SQL to SQL translation. 

2. While there are multiple prior works that explore the task of Natural Language to SQL generation the authors highlight that the task of SQL to SQL translation also significant practical utility for instance in the event of migrating an SQL query created for one database system such as MySQL into an equivalent query for another database system such as ClickHouse. The authors argue that existing SQL benchmarks are ill-suited for this task because they typically focus on a single system and fail to capture the complex, system-specific dialect differences (e.g. unique functions, data types, syntax rules) found in real-world scenarios.

3. To address this gap, the authors curate a diverse collection of real-world SQL queries from 38 open-source benchmarks and private enterprise workloads. This paper details the rigorous curation workflow employed to create a challenging and realistic dataset. Furthermore the author conduct experiments on the PARROT benchmark that suggest that LLMs like GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.7, DeepSeek R1 etc struggle with this task, highlighting significant room for improvement. 

**Contributions**
1. The authors release the PARROT benchmark with 3 variants
   - PARROT: 598 challenging, manually verified translation pairs from diverse, real-world sources.
   - PARROT-Diverse: 28,003 pairs across 22 database systems for extensive syntax and dialect testing.
   - PARROT-Simple: 5,306 simple, representative samples for focused stress-testing of specific translation rules.

2. The author's provide a rigorous data curation methodology including a 5 step workflow for creating the benchmark which includes
   - Collecting real-world SQL queries.
   - Standardizing and anonymizing data.
   - Filtering for complexity and diversity.
   - Using an ensemble of rule-based tools and LLMs for annotation.
   - Performing error-guided selection to ensure correctness.

3. The author's perform a experimental comparative analysis of open-sourced and closed LLMs on the benchmark and highlight the significant room for improvement on the benchmark

4. The authors release PARROT, along with its variants, source code, and a public leaderboard to facilitate future research.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The benchmark is novel and the first to introduce SQL to SQL translation task (as stated by authors and to the best of my knowledge). Current existing benchmarks such as BIRD have only looked at the Text to SQL translation tasks.
2. The benchmark offers practical utility as database migrations are common for enterprises and the task of automating the translation of SQL queries is particularly relevant in these cases. The benchmark also highlights the significant room for improvement in modern day LLMs for this task.
3. The paper is very well written. The data curation methodology is rigorous and methodical. The experimentation analysis with different open and closed source models is also well presented and sound.

Overall the paper is extremely strong and makes solid contributions to the field.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. An in-depth qualitative analysis of failure cases is lacking in the paper. It would be good to find common patterns of failure in modern day LLMs and present them in the Appendix for completeness
2. As an additional optional analysis the author's could include results of Gemini 2.5 pro in the comparison as it ranks number 1 on LMSYS for code.
3. As a part of the queries are derived from the public benchmarks it is possible that some LLMs may have been trained on the data. Therefore there is a risk that the benchmarks might be skewed towards measuring memorization in LLMs. Additional steps may be needed to transform the queries to be sufficiently distinct while retaining the semantics so as to avoid this.
4. The efficiency of the translated queries compared to the original queries is not measured in the benchmark. For instance in an edge case scenario the translated query might be much slower on the new DB system or may timeout or there might be other ways of rewriting the query to be more efficient. Having this additional signal would also provide a measure of quality of translation

The dataset code is available under here: https://github.com/weAIDB/PARROT
The code is well written and the dataset is available to download via hugging-face cli. 

The command/script/instructions to trigger the automatic-evalauation on the benchmark however seems to be missing. The authors should update the README with this command and the code with the script.

additional_feedback.value: The rebuttal strengthens the paper. Clarifying that Acc_{RES} compares full result sets over real databases rather than a few synthetic rows is important; please bake these specifics into §4 with per-dialect dataset descriptors (tables/row counts, result-equivalence tolerances for float/decimal, collation/NULL semantics, ordering guarantees) so that Acc_{EX}/Acc_{RES} are unambiguous and fully reproducible (see metric definitions already in §4: Acc_{EX} executability; Acc_{RES} strict result identity). Beyond the helpful failure taxonomy, consider publishing a feature-aligned error schema (functions, types, windowing, timezones, implicit cast rules) and mapping each item in PARROT/PARROT-Diverse/PARROT-Simple to those facets to enable per-capability leaderboards. Also: (i) add stratified splits and report stratified significance (bootstrap CIs across queries and dialects); (ii) release the evaluation harness with pinned seeds/versions and a "fail-fast" safety layer (read-only/SELECT-only execution + static guards); (iii) document the anonymization pipeline and contamination checks; (iv) release prompts/scripts for testcase generation used in semantic checking, even if the training rows themselves remain private; and (v) add guidance for multi-hop/bi-directional evaluation as optional tracks. Finally, since PARROT's core sets span 598 curated pairs (main), 28,003 diverse pairs, and 5,306 unit-style snippets across 22 systems, it would help to expose per-dialect coverage dashboards to show where headroom remains.

final_justification.value: I maintain Accept (5). The paper targets a timely, practically consequential task — cross-system SQL translation — that existing NL2SQL benchmarks cannot probe due to limited dialect diversity and system-specific phenomena. The benchmark composition (PARROT core + Diverse + Simple) is clearly described, with scope and scale appropriate for NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks, and the evaluation protocol is concrete (execution-first Acc_{EX}/Acc_{RES} with reference executors and schema normalization). Empirically, the paper documents sizeable performance gaps for strong models in both curated cross-dialect pairs and a real ByteHouse workload — evidence that the task is far from solved and that the resource will drive research. The rebuttal addresses my main concerns: it clarifies semantics evaluation at scale, adds a concrete failure taxonomy, expands baselines (RAG/SFT/hybrid with SQLGlot), and commits to language fixes and discussion of safety/robustness. Provided these clarifications (and the taxonomy visualization) are incorporated in the camera-ready, and the evaluation harness/prompts are released alongside the already announced leaderboard, the artifact will be high-leverage for both academic and industrial communities. My remaining suggestions (stratified significance; feature-aligned capability tags; explicit tolerance rules) are straightforward to integrate and will further increase diagnostic value. Overall, the contribution is well-motivated, carefully engineered, and demonstrably impactful; I recommend acceptance.

summary.value: This paper presents PARROT, a benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) in cross-system SQL translation (SQL-to-SQL). Unlike the widely studied Text-to-SQL task, SQL-to-SQL focuses on converting SQL queries from one database system dialect to another while preserving functionality. The authors curate the dataset from 38 public and proprietary sources (e.g., ByteDance), propose a five-stage curation workflow, and conduct comprehensive evaluations on multiple LLMs. PARROT includes variants (PARROT, PARROT-Diverse, PARROT-Simple) and introduces dual metrics for syntactic correctness and semantic fidelity.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper addresses a practically important yet underexplored task—cross-dialect SQL translation—which is critical for enterprise-level database migration, system interoperability, and real-world automation.

- Novel benchmark focus: PARROT is the first benchmark specifically designed for SQL-to-SQL translation, filling a notable gap between Text-to-SQL and rule-based SQL conversion tools.

- Diverse, high-quality dataset: The authors compile 33,000+ SQL pairs spanning 22 dialects. The use of both open benchmarks and industrial SQLs (ByteHouse) adds realism and diversity.

- Rigorous curation pipeline: The 5-step processing pipeline (data standardization, clustering, ensemble annotation, error-guided filtering, serialization) demonstrates strong engineering effort and replicable methodology.

- Comprehensive experiments: Benchmarking across proprietary and open-source LLMs reveals critical performance gaps (e.g., hallucinations, inability to handle NULLs or date formats). The case study (Table 4) is especially illustrative.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The case study is strong, but a taxonomy of common failure modes (e.g., date parsing, alias scope errors, aggregate translation) with frequencies could offer deeper insights.
2. Although the dataset is used to evaluate many LLMs, the authors provide limited discussion on how prompt engineering or decoding strategies impact results.
3. The Acc_RES metric assumes fully aligned schemas, but the paper lacks details on how schema differences, type coercion, or NULL handling are managed. In practice, cross-system translation often involves schema mismatches and differences in NULL semantics. Clarifying these aspects would improve reproducibility.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The repository is well-organized and contains sufficient material to replicate the core results. The JSON-format serialization, translation type taxonomy, and sample prompts enhance usability for benchmarking and system development. The use of ANTLR and SQLGlot makes the pipeline technically robust and extensible.

final_justification.value: The authors have addressed most of the reviewers' concerns. I hope that the authors will further review the relevant work in final version.

title.value: PARROT: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Cross-System SQL Translation

abstract.value: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing effectiveness in Text-to-SQL tasks. However, another closely related problem, Cross-System SQL Translation (a.k.a., SQL-to-SQL), which adapts a query written for one database system (e.g., MySQL) into its equivalent one for another system (e.g., ClickHouse), is of great practical importance but remains underexplored. Existing SQL benchmarks are not well-suited for SQL-to-SQL evaluation, which (1) focus on a limited set of database systems (often just SQLite) and (2) cannot capture many system-specific SQL dialects (e.g., customized functions, data types, and syntax rules). Thus, in this paper, we introduce PARROT, a Practical And Realistic BenchmaRk for CrOss-System SQL Translation. PARROT comprises 598 translation pairs from 38 open-source benchmarks and real-world business services, specifically prepared to challenge system-specific SQL understanding (e.g., LLMS achieve lower than 38.53% accuracy on average). We also provide multiple benchmark variants, including PARROT-Diverse with 28,003 translation (for extensive syntax testing) and PARROT-Simple with 5,306 representative samples (for focused stress testing), covering 22 production-grade database systems. To promote future research, we release a public leaderboard and source code at: https://code4db.github.io/parrot-bench/.

If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
